quran.note: Knowledge given to Dawud and Sulayman; the language of birds; the valley of the ants.
Sulayman as one who turned back to Allah, and his prayer for a kingdom.
The wind, the jinn at work, and how his death was discovered.
The Qur’an itself clears Sulayman of disbelief.

hadith.summary: The Prophet ﷺ said Sulayman once resolved to go to his wives in a single night so that each would bear a rider fighting for Allah, but he did not add “if Allah wills”. Only one conceived, and she bore a child in an incomplete form. Had he said it, the Prophet ﷺ said, they would all have fought for Allah’s cause.
hadith.note: The number of wives differs between narrations; the sunnah.com page for this report notes a variant of ninety.

hadith.summary: The Prophet ﷺ said a powerful jinn tried to break his prayer and Allah let him overpower it. He thought of tying it to a mosque pillar, then remembered his brother Sulayman’s prayer for a kingdom no one after him would have, and let it go.

The Prophet ﷺ said that when Sulayman finished building Bayt al-Maqdis he asked Allah for three things: judgment that matches Allah’s, a kingdom no one after him would have, and that whoever comes to that mosque only to pray in it leaves free of sin.
The same report from Abdullah ibn Amr; Ibn Majah’s version records the Prophet ﷺ saying he hoped the third request had also been granted.

The Prophet ﷺ told of two women and a wolf that took one woman’s child. Dawud ruled for the elder; Sulayman asked for a knife to divide the living child, and the younger woman’s cry showed who the mother was.

scholarly.work: Tafsir Ibn Kathir (abridged English edition, read on Quran.com)
scholarly.author: Ibn Kathir
scholarly.summary: Reads “Sulayman inherited Dawud” as inheriting kingship and prophethood, not wealth, and cites the saying that prophets leave nothing to be inherited.

scholarly.work: Tafsir Ibn Kathir (abridged English edition, read on Quran.com)
scholarly.author: Ibn Kathir
scholarly.summary: Gives no explanation of the “body” placed on Sulayman’s throne beyond saying that Allah tried him, then he turned back to Allah.

scholarly.work: Tafsir Ibn Kathir (abridged English edition, read on Quran.com)
scholarly.author: Ibn Kathir
scholarly.summary: Says the wind carried him a month’s journey out and a month back, and relates a report of al-Hasan al-Basri that it went from Damascus to Istakhar to Kabul in a day and a night. The abridged text gives no grading for that report.

scholarly.work: Tafsir Ibn Kathir (abridged English edition, read on Quran.com)
scholarly.author: Ibn Kathir
scholarly.summary: Relates, from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah and others, that Sulayman stayed leaning on his staff for a long time, nearly a year, after he had died, until a creature of the earth ate the staff. The jinn then saw that they did not know the unseen. The abridged text does not grade these reports.

differences.question: What did Sulayman do to the horses (38:31-33)?

views.work: Tafsir Ibn Kathir (abridged English edition, read on Quran.com)
views.view: He ordered the horses slaughtered, in anger for Allah’s sake, because they had made him miss the Asr prayer.

views.work: Tafsir Ibn Kathir (abridged English edition, read on Quran.com)
views.view: The horses’ necks and hamstrings were struck with swords.

views.who: Ibn Abbas, preferred by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari
views.work: Tafsir Ibn Kathir (abridged English edition, read on Quran.com)
views.view: He began to pat their heads and legs out of love for them. The abridged text says Ibn Jarir favoured this because Sulayman would not punish animals for his own distraction, and adds that this preference is subject to further review.

differences.note: The Saheeh International translation printed in this app renders the verse as “striking their legs and necks”; Ma’ariful Qur’an’s translation reads “rub down their legs and necks”. The Arabic is the same.

differences.question: What was the “body” placed on his throne (38:34)?

views.who: Leave it as the Qur’an leaves it
views.work: Ma’ariful Qur’an (English edition, read on Quran.com), on 38:34
views.view: Ma’ariful Qur’an follows Ibn Kathir in not fixing the detail: Allah tried Sulayman and he turned back to Allah the more. It says “let these be entrusted with Allah”.

views.who: The incomplete-child report applied to the verse
views.work: Ma’ariful Qur’an (English edition, read on Quran.com), on 38:34
views.view: Some commentators apply the hadith of the wives (Sahih al-Bukhari 3424). Ma’ariful Qur’an notes that no hadith links the two and that Bukhari did not place it under this verse.

views.work: Ma’ariful Qur’an (English edition, read on Quran.com), on 38:34
views.view: That Sulayman was so weakened by illness that he lay like a body without a soul. Ma’ariful Qur’an calls this conjecture with little support in the wording or in hadith.

differences.question: Who brought the throne of Saba (27:40)?

views.work: Tafsir Ibn Kathir (abridged English edition, read on Quran.com), on 27:38-40

views.who: Muhammad ibn Ishaq (via Yazid ibn Ruman)
views.work: Tafsir Ibn Kathir (abridged English edition, read on Quran.com), on 27:38-40
views.view: Asif ibn Barkhiya, a truthful believer who knew the Greatest Name of Allah.

views.work: Tafsir Ibn Kathir (abridged English edition, read on Quran.com), on 27:38-40
views.view: A believer among the humans, named Asif.

differences.note: The Qur’an says only “one who had knowledge of the Book”. The abridged text lists the three views without ranking them.
